gap: No result ChatGPT got states, side by side, how much of each unit's headline wattage one 120 V leg can carry: Anker's 6,000 W F3800 Plus is capped at 25 A on its L14-30R (3,000 W per leg), while Pecron's 7,200 W F5000LFP is 3,600 W × 2 and Jackery's 7,200 W is 30 A at 240 V with two 3,600 W 120 V banks. A 5,000 W load is therefore a 240 V or balanced-leg load on every one of them, with about 1,000 W to spare on the Anker and 2,200 W on the 7,200 W units.
standout_why: Compared against solarwaypoint.com and holdbackup.com (both cited), ankersolix.com/f3800-plus (cited), powerbencher.com, thewattguide.com and thiswatt.com. Solar Waypoint gives no per-outlet or per-leg figure and no end-of-life percentage for cycle life. HoldBackup already normalises cycle life (Anker 3,000+ to 80%, EcoFlow Delta Pro Ultra 3,500 to 80%, Jackery 4,000 to 70%) and gives the Delta Pro Ultra's 10-second surge, so that half of the angle is taken. Anker's own page carries the raw 25 A / 6,000 W L14-30R line. TheWattGuide (returned, not cited) already has Jackery's two 3,600 W 120 V banks. ChatGPT's answer itself says a 7,200 W total does not mean one 120 V socket supplies 5,000 W, and that 5,000 W is about 21 A at 240 V. What none has is the per-leg figures for the line-up in one table with headroom at 5,000 W, and Pecron's 3,600 W × 2. I could not source the per-leg figure for our own Nature's Generator L6000, which weakens it further.
decides: It confirms rather than changes the pick. A 7,200 W / 30 A unit (Jackery Explorer 5000 Plus, $3,499, flagged available in Jackery's store search record) runs a 5,000 W 240 V load with about 2,200 W spare and takes 3,600 W on either 120 V leg. The 6,000 W / 25 A Anker F3800 Plus runs it with about 1,000 W spare and 3,000 W per leg, so an unbalanced panel trips it sooner. The Pecron matches the Jackery at $2,399 but is a pre-order shipping early January, more than four weeks out. The EcoFlow Delta Pro Ultra reads unavailable, and the Titan 5000 Plus is a pre-order shipping late January. Our Nature's Generator L6000 ($2,249.99, flagged available) is the lowest-priced unit I could read that states 6,000 W continuous at 120/240 V. As a 6,000 W split-phase unit it would be 3,000 W per leg by arithmetic, but its store pages returned 429, so its per-outlet, surge and cycle-life figures are not maker-sourced here. The page should not claim per-leg parity with the 7,200 W units for it.
